title: Saleable Product Rules - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Understand the tax rules governing a Saleable Product generated during experimental R&D trials in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: A saleable product, in Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program, matters to taxpayers claiming materials consumed or transformed in eligible work performed in Canada. Those materials qualify at 100%, but if resulting SR&ED property, such as a transformed material prototype, is sold or converted to commercial use, Income Tax Act subsections 127(27) to 127(36) recapture claimed benefits.

body.text: A saleable product, in Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program, matters to taxpayers claiming materials consumed or transformed in eligible work performed in Canada. Those materials qualify at 100%, but if resulting SR&ED property, such as a transformed material prototype, is sold or converted to commercial use, Income Tax Act subsections 127(27) to 127(36) recapture claimed benefits.

Between December 2024 and November 2026, Parliament enacted the largest structural expansion of the federal SR&ED program in more than a decade. Under Bill C-15 (the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3, implementing the Budget 2025 tax measures), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, four major statutory reforms took effect retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024: doubling the annual Expenditure Limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual enhanced refundable credit from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000); widening the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000; extending the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a $15,000,000–$75,000,000 three-year average gross revenue phase-out (which Canadian-controlled private corporations [CCPCs] may also elect to apply); and restoring both Section 37 income deductibility and Section 127 ITC eligibility for SR&ED capital expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) acquired after December 15, 2024. Administratively, on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process inside My Business Account, delivering upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks.

Subsequently, Federal Budget 2026 (Masters of our Destiny), tabled on November 5, 2026 by Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne, omitted a previously promised federal Patent Box regime for the second consecutive budget. Rather than enacting an income-based Patent Box, the federal government confirmed the permanent Productivity Mega Deduction (immediate 100% capital expensing across more than 65% of business investments, including patents) and proposed a $930,000,000 five-year ($235,000,000 ongoing annual) expansion of SR&ED—applicable to expenditures incurred in taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026—to cover initial regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs linked to eligible SR&ED projects, subject to recapture upon IP disposition. Across the provinces, Québec replaced eight legacy innovation measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 with the fully refundable Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation (CRIC—30% on the first $1,000,000 above an exclusion threshold and 20% thereafter) while replacing its e-business credit (CDAE) with the artificial-intelligence-focused CDAEIA after December 31, 2025, and British Columbia harmonized its 10% provincial SR&ED credit with the federal $6,000,000 limit, $15,000,000–$75,000,000 phase-out, capital restoration, and ECPC refundability rules.
1. Macro-Fiscal Profile, Governing Authorities, and Legislative Chronology
1.1 Institutional Architecture and National Program Scale

Canada's federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Program operates under a dual-agency governance structure separating tax policy legislation from operational audit administration. The Department of Finance Canada drafts statutory amendments to the Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), the "ITA") and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, the "Regulations"), conducts pre-budget consultations, and publishes annual tax expenditure projections. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the program nationwide—publishing official eligibility and financial policies, maintaining Form T661 and Guide T4088, managing the My Business Account SR&ED client portal, conducting technical scientific reviews and financial audits, and issuing corporate assessments and cash refunds.

Unlike discretionary innovation grants or contribution agreements—such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), CanExport, or Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's (ISED) Strategic Response Fund (formerly the Strategic Innovation Fund)—the SR&ED incentive is a non-discretionary statutory entitlement under the ITA. There is no competitive intake window, fixed annual appropriation cap, or ministerial selection committee; every taxpayer performing qualifying work in Canada and filing complete prescribed forms within the statutory 18-month reporting window is legally entitled to the deduction and credit.

According to figures compiled from the Department of Finance Canada's Report on Federal Tax Expenditures 2026 (Part 2), the federal SR&ED investment tax credit represented an estimated public fiscal cost of $5,176,000,000 ($5.176 billion) in calendar year 2025, making it Canada's largest single non-dilutive innovation program. Official CRA SR&ED program statistics for federal fiscal years 2021/22 through 2025/26 (running April 1 to March 31, as compiled in October 2026 statistical releases) document sustained growth in claim volume and dollar value. Between fiscal years 2021/22 and 2025/26, annual SR&ED claims filed rose 18.8% from 20,332 to 24,160, while total ITCs claimed rose 44.1% from $3.4 billion to $4.9 billion—lifting the calculated average claim sought from roughly $167,000 to roughly $203,000. In fiscal year 2025/26, the CRA allowed $4.6 billion of the $4.9 billion claimed, with 59.0% of allowed credits paid out as refundable credits and 41.0% applied or carried over as non-refundable credits.

body.text: Breaking down CRA fiscal year 2025/26 statistics by claimant enterprise size (measured by gross income) highlights a sharp contrast between filing frequency and credit concentration. Small businesses with gross income under $4,000,000 filed 65% of all claims processed but received 33% of total ITCs allowed; businesses with $4,000,000 to $20,000,000 in gross income filed 20% of claims and captured 23% of allowed ITCs; mid-to-large businesses with $20,000,000 to $250,000,000 in gross income filed 12% of claims and received 22% of allowed ITCs; and large corporations exceeding $250,000,000 in gross income filed only 3% of claims while capturing 22% of all ITCs allowed. Across scientific disciplines, software development is now the single largest technical field, expanding from 35.7% of allowed credits in 2021/22 to 42.6% in 2025/26—representing an increase calculated from rounded CRA aggregates from roughly $1.18 billion to roughly $1.96 billion (up approximately 66% over four years, compared with roughly 24% across all other scientific fields combined).
1.2 Chronology of Legislative Reforms (December 2024 to November 2026)

Auditors and tax advisers reviewing corporate filings for 2024 through 2027 must carefully separate superseded 2024–2025 draft proposals, enacted law under Bill C-15, and prospective proposals tabled in Budget 2026. Relying on outdated tax alerts that cite an interim $4,500,000 expenditure cap or assume enactment of a federal Patent Box is a major compliance hazard.

In the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (tabled December 16, 2024 under the previous Trudeau administration) and subsequent draft legislation released by the Department of Finance in August 2025, Ottawa initially proposed raising the enhanced 35% ITC Expenditure Limit from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, widening taxable capital phase-out thresholds to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extending the enhanced refundable credit to ECPCs, restoring pre-2014 capital expenditure eligibility, and introducing a federal Patent Box tax regime. When the Carney government presented Federal Budget 2025 on November 4, 2025, it superseded the $4,500,000 proposal by doubling the enhanced Expenditure Limit directly from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, while omitting any Patent Box measure. Bill C-15 (the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, enacting the $6,000,000 limit, the $15,000,000–$75,000,000 phase-out band, ECPC eligibility, the CCPC gross-revenue phase-out election, and capital expenditure restoration retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (and depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024).

On September 15, 2026, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced—and Budget 2026 subsequently confirmed—the permanent Productivity Mega Deduction, enabling businesses to immediately write off 100% of the full cost of a broad range of depreciable capital assets (estimated by Finance Canada, as reported in practitioner summaries, to cover more than 65% of business investment, including patents alongside machinery and infrastructure, lowering Canada's marginal effective tax rate on new business investment from 13% to 6.4%, with asset-by-asset eligibility to be confirmed once legislation is tabled). Policy trackers emphasize that the Productivity Mega Deduction is a cost-based Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) immediate-expensing measure, not an income-based Patent Box preference.

On November 5, 2026, Minister François-Philippe Champagne tabled Federal Budget 2026 (Masters of our Destiny). Budget 2026 again omitted a federal Patent Box or any Notice of Ways and Means Motion for preferential IP income taxation. Instead, Budget 2026 proposed expanding the SR&ED program itself—for expenditures incurred in taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026—to cover initial regulatory certification studies and IP registration/maintenance expenses tied to eligible SR&ED projects. Alongside this proposed SR&ED expansion, Budget 2026 confirmed multi-year IP ecosystem funding ($75,000,000 over three years starting in 2026–27 to extend the NRC IP Assist Program and $22,500,000 over three years starting in 2026–27 for the Innovation Asset Collective's Patent Collective, complementing Budget 2025's $84,400,000 over four years for ISED's Elevate IP program), announced a Federal Intellectual Property Review and new Patent Act regulations establishing minimum standards for written patent demand letters, added $1,000,000,000 over six years starting in 2028–29 to the Strategic Response Fund, introduced the Canada Growth Incentive (an exemption on up to $15,000,000 of capital gains from qualifying Canadian company investments plus a three-year extension on small business share rollover reinvestments for dispositions on or after January 1, 2027), and launched consultations due January 8, 2027 on permitting corporate loss transfers within wholly owned corporate groups.

body.text: 2. Statutory Eligibility of R&D Work and Binding Jurisprudence
2.1 Subsection 248(1) Definition and the CRA Why and How Guidelines

Technical eligibility for federal SR&ED incentives is governed by the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Historically codified in Regulation 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations before moving without material substantive alteration to subsection 248(1) of the ITA, the Act defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis".

Within that statutory framework, qualifying SR&ED encompasses three core categories of investigation alongside directly commensurate support work: basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with no specific practical application in view; applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and experimental development (paragraph 248(1)(c)), defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for creating new materials, devices, products, or processes, or improving existing ones, including incremental improvements. Activities directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting those core investigations qualify when commensurate with the underlying R&D, whereas routine commercial development, quality control, and routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes are statutorily excluded.

Having archived its older Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (as examined in August 2022 legal commentary), the CRA now structures its administrative review guidelines around two cumulative statutory requirements—the "Why" and the "How"—derived directly from subsection 248(1). The "Why" requirement asks whether the work was conducted to advance scientific knowledge or achieve a technological advancement—requiring the claimant to identify a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty that could not be resolved through standard practice or routine engineering. CRA guidelines specify seven objective indicators demonstrating that existing scientific or engineering knowledge is insufficient: existing design methods are inapplicable; requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards; there are too many variables or unknowns; parameters or conditions lie outside the normal operating range; the nature of the problem is evolving; data is not readily available; or interlocking constraints block standard solutions.

Complementing the technological objective, the "How" requirement asks whether the work was carried out via a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Under CRA administrative policy, satisfying the "How" test requires four documented operational stages: (1) generating a hypothesis—an idea consistent with known facts serving as a starting point for investigation toward resolving the problem; (2) testing that hypothesis or proposed method through experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve iteratively in response to test data; (3) developing logical conclusions grounded in experimental or analytical findings; and (4) keeping contemporaneous evidence generated naturally as the work progresses.
2.2 Foundational Case Law and Federal Court of Appeal Precedents

Because the text of subsection 248(1) is concise, Canadian appellate courts have articulated binding evidentiary and methodological tests governing SR&ED audits. The cornerstone judicial authority in Canada is Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (Tax Court of Canada), in which Justice Donald Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court) formulated at paragraph 16 a five-question cumulative test that every project must satisfy to qualify as SR&ED:

items: Was there a technological (or technical) risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or habitual procedures?
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?

Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline (established and objective principles) of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?
Did the process result in a technological advance, that is to say an advancement in the general understanding?
Did the taxpayer keep a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed?

body.text: The Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) promptly elevated Justice Bowman's five questions to binding national precedent in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, (1998) 99 D.T.C. 5087, 235 N.R. 258 (FCA, December 21, 1998). Evaluating R&D performed under a December 1, 1982 agreement to develop a concrete forming medium for cast-in-situ concrete construction, the FCA endorsed the Northwest Hydraulic approach at paragraph 10 and ordered the Minister to reassess and allow the taxpayer's SR&ED deduction, research allowance, and ITC. Three years later, in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (Docket A-601-00, December 11, 2001, per Sexton J.A.), the FCA examined 1991–1995 software claims by a global lottery marketer handling two to three million customers and up to 25,000 daily multilingual computer and telephone transactions. Affirming Judge Bonner's Tax Court decision (which preferred the Crown expert's evidence), the FCA confirmed at paragraph 17 that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria govern software development and upheld disallowance where complex commercial software engineering lacked qualifying SR&ED uncertainty and methodology. The FCA subsequently reaffirmed Northwest Hydraulic after the SR&ED definition moved from the Regulations into ITA subsection 248(1), notably in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355 (at para. 6) and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada, 2016 FCA 152 (at para. 4).

In 2021 and 2022, the FCA decisively rejected taxpayer attempts to narrow Justice Bowman's third criterion. In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (Docket A-442-19, May 10, 2021, per Webb J.A., Near and Boivin JJ.A. concurring), a taxpayer reassessed for its 2009 and 2010 taxation years contended that because the text of subsection 248(1) contains no explicit reference to "scientific method," the Tax Court erred in requiring adherence to the scientific method under Criterion 3. Dismissing the appeal with costs fixed at $1,670, the FCA held that Justice Bowman's five criteria properly interpret the statutory definition of SR&ED under settled appellate precedent (RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, Jentel, and R&D Pro-Innovation). Similarly, in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (Docket A-231-20, May 3, 2022, per Rennie J.A., Woods and Laskin JJ.A. concurring; leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed March 9, 2023), the FCA dismissed an R&D consulting firm's appeal, holding that Kam-Press settled the applicability of the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion and upholding the Tax Court's denial—even without an expert report—where the appellant did not conduct its work methodically and kept records judged "vague," "unclear," and failing to reflect "a logical progression between the premise of an experiment and the result". At the Tax Court level, Airzone One Ltd. v. The Queen explicitly bridged jurisprudence and current CRA policy by linking Northwest Hydraulic Questions 1 and 4 to the "Why" requirement and Questions 2, 3, and 5 to the "How" requirement, allowing Airzone's projects where developing entirely new analytical protocols demonstrated non-routine technological advancement.

body.text: 3. Federal Deduction Pool, Credit Rates, Expenditure Caps, and Refundability
3.1 Section 37 Income Deduction Pool vs. Section 127 Investment Tax Credit

Under the Canadian federal income tax system, qualifying R&D benefits from two complementary statutory mechanisms: (1) an immediate 100% deduction against business income (with pooling of undeducted balances) under section 37 of the ITA, and (2) an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) computed under section 127 and refunded (where eligible) under section 127.1 of the ITA.

Under subsection 37(1), taxpayers carrying on business in Canada deduct allowable SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada—comprising current expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a) and, as restored by Bill C-15 for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, eligible capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b). Subsection 37(8) sets out the interpretive rules governing which expenditures qualify under subsection 37(1) in respect of SR&ED in Canada (including amended subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II) and paragraph 37(8)(e) extending eligibility to capital property acquired and equipment lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024), contrasted with subsection 37(2), which governs current deductions for R&D conducted outside Canada. Where SR&ED is performed on a taxpayer's behalf or through third-party entities, subsection 37(14) formerly imposed a statutory look-through rule limiting third-party/contracted inclusions to expenditures of a current nature; Bill C-15 repealed it, consequential on the addition of paragraph 37(1)(b), for property acquired, and lease costs first becoming payable, on or after December 16, 2024.
3.2 Claimant Classifications: CCPCs, ECPCs, Foreign Subsidiaries, and Unincorporated Entities

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, federal ITC rates and cash refundability for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 depend on whether the taxpayer falls into one of four statutory categories under subsections 127(5), 127(8), 127(9), 127(10.1), 127(10.7), 127(10.8), and section 127.1 (with transitional definitions under subsections 127(9.01) and 127(9.02), and tax-exempt entities excluded under subsection 149(1)):

Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) earn an enhanced 35% ITC (comprising the 15% basic "specified percentage" under subsection 127(9) plus an additional 20% under subsection 127(10.1)) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual Expenditure Limit, and earn the 15% basic ITC on qualified expenditures exceeding that limit.

Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—a new statutory category defined in subsection 127(9) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—likewise earn the 35% enhanced refundable ITC up to their annual Expenditure Limit (and a 15% non-refundable ITC above that limit). To qualify as an ECPC, a corporation must satisfy three conditions throughout the taxation year: (1) be resident in Canada; (2) have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or, if not listed, have validly elected or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue to be a public corporation); and (3) not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. In addition, Canadian-resident subsidiary corporations where all or substantially all (90% or more) of the shares of capital stock are owned by one or more ECPCs also qualify for the enhanced refundable credit. Prior to Bill C-15, listing on a public exchange immediately stripped Canadian innovators of the 35% refundable credit; ECPCs now retain refundable support through post-IPO growth.

Other Corporations—including Canadian subsidiaries controlled by foreign multinationals, non-qualifying public corporations, and CCPCs or ECPCs whose Expenditure Limit has completely phased out above $75,000,000—earn the 15% basic non-refundable ITC on all qualified SR&ED expenditures with no upper dollar ceiling. For example, on $800,000 of qualified current SR&ED spending, a foreign-controlled private subsidiary earns $120,000 (15%) strictly as a non-refundable tax offset, whereas a qualifying CCPC or ECPC within its limit earns $280,000 (35%) as a cash refund.

Individuals (Sole Proprietorships), Partnerships, and Trusts earn the 15% basic ITC. Individuals and qualifying trusts are eligible for 40% cash refundability on unused 15% ITCs remaining after offsetting federal Part I tax owing, whereas partnership ITCs are governed by subsection 127(8) and allocated to partners.
3.3 Expenditure Limits, Phase-Out Thresholds, and the CCPC Revenue Election

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the maximum annual Expenditure Limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000—unlocking up to $2,100,000 per year in enhanced federal credits ($6,000,000 × 35%, compared to $1,050,000 previously). Associated CCPCs must share a single $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit across all CCPCs in the associated corporate group (with special allocation rules applying where an associated CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year). Similarly, ECPCs must share the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit across all members of a consolidated group preparing consolidated financial statements as a single economic entity. Under subsection 127(10.5), any corporation with a short taxation year must prorate its Expenditure Limit by multiplying the base limit by the ratio of days in the short taxation year to 365 (for instance, CRA policy illustrates subsection 127(10.5) proration for a 184-day taxation year from July 1 to December 31 using [184 ÷ 365], which yields $1,512,328 on a $3,000,000 base or $3,024,658 on the enacted $6,000,000 base).
Two statutory phase-out tests govern the gradual reduction of the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024:

Under the default CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out (ITA subsection 127(10.2)), a CCPC's $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit begins to decrease once the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (combined across all associated CCPCs) for the previous taxation year reaches $15,000,000, and becomes nil ($0) once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000 or more (replacing the pre-December 16, 2024 thresholds of $10,000,000 and $50,000,000).

Under the ECPC Gross Revenue Phase-Out and CCPC Election (ITA subsections 127(10.6), 127(10.31) and 127(10.32)), an ECPC's $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit begins to decrease once its average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (determined from consolidated financial statements if part of a consolidated group, including entities joining or leaving during the year) reaches $15,000,000, and becomes nil ($0) at $75,000,000 or greater. Crucially, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC may file a prescribed election to calculate its Expenditure Limit using this three-year average annual gross revenue method instead of prior-year taxable capital (summing the three-year average annual financial-statement revenues of all corporations in the associated group for the taxation year, regardless of whether they were associated throughout all three preceding years). Where an associated CCPC group makes this election, the subsection 127(10.2) taxable capital reduction does not apply for that year—protecting pre-revenue or low-revenue biotechnology, cleantech, and deep-tech CCPCs that hold more than $15,000,000 in balance-sheet capital.
3.4 Refundability Nuances, Carryovers, Control Changes, and ITC Recapture

Auditors verifying corporate cash refunds under section 127.1 must distinguish between a CCPC that meets the definition of a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) and one governed by subsection 127.1(2.01). Under CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC's Qualifying Income Limit under subsection 127.1(2) is calculated using the updated formula:

where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is ≤ $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 (replacing the pre-December 16, 2024 $40,000,000 denominator and $10,000,000 threshold). A CCPC meeting the "qualifying corporation" definition under subsection 127.1(2) receives 100% cash refundability on its 35% ITC for current expenditures up to its Expenditure Limit, 40% cash refundability on its 35% ITC for capital expenditures up to its Expenditure Limit, and 40% cash refundability on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures exceeding its Expenditure Limit. If a CCPC is neither a qualifying corporation nor an excluded corporation (because prior-year taxable income exceeded its Qualifying Income Limit), subsection 127.1(2.01) still grants 100% refundability on its 35% current-expenditure ITC and 40% refundability on its 35% capital-expenditure ITC within its Expenditure Limit, but any 15% ITC earned above its Expenditure Limit is 0% refundable. For ECPCs, 15% ITCs earned on current or capital expenditures in excess of the annual Expenditure Limit are strictly non-refundable.

Under subsection 127.1(3), refunded ITCs are deemed to have been deducted against federal Part I tax payable in the taxation year. Unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back 3 preceding taxation years (limited to the lesser of the undeducted current-year ITC and prior-year Part I tax otherwise payable in excess of prior-year ITCs) and carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years under subsections 127(5) and 127(9). Where a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control, statutory rules restrict both the carryforward of pre-acquisition unused ITCs and the carryback of post-acquisition ITCs. Finally, under subsections 127(27) to 127(36), if a claimant sells SR&ED property (including capital equipment or transformed material prototypes) or converts it from SR&ED use to commercial use, ITC recapture rules apply to recover previously claimed SR&ED tax benefits.

body.text: 4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methods, and Capital Property Rules
4.1 Salaries, Wages, Specified Employees, and Permissible Foreign Work

Salaries and wages represent the largest qualifying expenditure pool for most Canadian claimants. Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, eligible remuneration rules differ substantially between regular (arm's-length) employees and specified employees, and between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method.

For regular (non-specified) employees, allowable direct SR&ED remuneration includes salary or wages incurred on or in respect of SR&ED, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, employment inducements or non-competition payments (considered remuneration for services rendered during employment, subject to exceptions), and taxable benefits. Cash outlays for taxable benefits qualify directly, while non-cash taxable benefits qualify only if three cumulative conditions are satisfied: (1) the benefit value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs; (2) the value excludes any Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax (GST/HST) or Provincial Sales Tax (PST) unless no input tax credit can be claimed; and (3) the actual costs to which the non-cash benefit relates are not separately claimed as a business expense. Under the Proxy Method, only salary or wages for employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada are included, and bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits are excluded from the salary base used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). Under the Traditional Method, salary or wages for employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED qualify as direct labour, while administrative salary or wages directly attributable to SR&ED may be claimed under SR&ED overhead.

A specified employee is an employee who is a "specified shareholder" (owning 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, counting shares owned by persons not dealing at arm's length with the employee) or someone related to a specified shareholder, such as a spouse, brother, or sister. Specified employees are subject to two strict statutory caps. First, in computing direct allowable SR&ED wages, all bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are excluded, and the specified employee's maximum claimable SR&ED salary is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE). Attempting to claim an owner-manager's $250,000+ compensation or bonus at face value without applying specified-employee caps results in routine audit disallowance. Second, when computing the 55% PPA salary base under the Proxy Method, Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8) further restrict a specified employee's proxy salary base to a maximum of 75% and 2.5 times the YMPE.

Although SR&ED must generally be conducted inside Canada, subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA permit claiming permissible salaries or wages of employees performing SR&ED work outside Canada, strictly capped at 10% of the salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada (and excluded from the Canadian proxy salary base).
4.2 Overhead Calculation Elections: Proxy Method (55% PPA) vs. Traditional Method

Taxpayers elect on Form T661 between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method to account for SR&ED overhead expenditures. Under the Proxy Method, governed by Regulation 2900(4), the claimant does not itemize actual overhead bills; instead, it computes a Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of its eligible Canadian proxy salary base (the proxy rate having been stepped down from 65% to 55% over a two-year period starting in 2013). Consequently, $1.00 of eligible regular Canadian base SR&ED salary generates $1.55 of federal qualified expenditures for ITC calculation purposes—delivering an effective 54.25% refundable federal credit ($1.55 × 35%) for CCPCs and ECPCs within their $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit, or 23.25% ($1.55 × 15%) at the basic corporate rate, prior to provincial R&D credits.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, no 55% PPA is calculated; the claimant instead tracks and substantiates actual overhead and other current expenditures (including directly attributable administrative wages) that are directly related to the SR&ED and incremental—meaning costs that would not have been incurred but for the SR&ED work.
4.3 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Contracts, Materials, and Cloud/Software Costs

Payments to arm's-length Canadian contractors performing eligible SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf are subject to a statutory 20% haircut for ITC purposes: 80% of the eligible contract amount enters qualified SR&ED expenditures (yielding an effective 80% × 35% = 28.0% enhanced refundable federal credit or 80% × 15% = 12.0% basic credit). Payments to foreign (non-Canadian) contractors performing work outside Canada are 0% eligible.

Payments to non-arm's-length contractors are restricted and cannot simply be claimed at 80% by the payer. Instead, non-arm's-length performers may transfer qualified SR&ED expenditures to the payer using Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, reported by the payer on Form T661 Line 510), while excess assistance within a non-arm's-length group is allocated via Form T1145 (reported on Line 540).

Claimants may include 100% of the cost of materials consumed or transformed in performing eligible SR&ED in Canada, subject to ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) if resulting property is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use. With respect to cloud computing and software costs, Canadian federal legislation has not created a standalone cloud-computing QRE category, and official CRA releases do not establish a special cloud super-deduction; accordingly, software licences, cloud compute, and hardware must satisfy the existing statutory rules—qualifying either as overhead (absorbed into the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method, or claimed only if proven directly related and strictly incremental under the Traditional Method) or, where depreciable hardware is acquired or leased after December 15, 2024, under the restored capital expenditure and equipment lease rules.
4.4 Restored Capital Expenditures (ASA) and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE)

Under Bill C-15 (amending ITA paragraph 37(1)(b), subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II), paragraph 37(8)(e), subsection 127(9), and subsection 127.1(2)), pre-2014 capital eligibility rules were reinstated for depreciable property acquired (available for use) after December 15, 2024 and equipment lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024; property acquired before December 16, 2024 remains strictly ineligible. Two distinct capital regimes now operate on the revised May 15, 2026 Form T661:

All or Substantially All (ASA — ≥90%) SR&ED Capital Property (Form T661 Line 390) applies to new or used depreciable property where, at acquisition, the taxpayer intended either to use all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life in performing SR&ED in Canada, or to consume 90% or more of its value in performing SR&ED in Canada. Allowable ASA capital expenditures on Line 390 combine with allowable current expenditures (Line 380) to form Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures on Line 400, and must not be claimed on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance). Buildings, land, rights to use buildings or land, inventory, and goodwill are excluded. Crucially, while used depreciable property meeting the 90% ASA test is deductible on Line 390, used equipment is a prescribed expenditure disallowed from earning the SR&ED ITC and must be backed out on Line 532 (alongside backing out capital outlays tied to tax-exempt income on Line 535). For CCPCs and ECPCs earning the 35% enhanced rate within their Expenditure Limit, eligible new ASA capital expenditures are 40% refundable (35% × 40% = 14.0% cash refund plus 21.0% non-refundable ITC).

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Form T661 Line 504) applies to new depreciable equipment (other than Prescribed Depreciable Property [PDP]) acquired (available for use) after December 15, 2024 that falls below the 90% ASA threshold but is used primarily (more than 50% of operating time, i.e., >50% to <90%) for SR&ED in Canada alongside commercial operations. SUE applies strictly for SR&ED ITC purposes: SUE capital cost is not added to the Section 37 SR&ED deduction pool and must instead be depreciated under standard CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8. The maximum SR&ED ITC on SUE is earned on 50% of the capital cost across two periods reported on Line 504: 25% for first-term SUE (the period starting at acquisition and ending at the end of the first taxation year that is at least 12 months after acquisition) and 25% for second-term SUE (the period starting at acquisition and ending at the end of the taxation year that is at least 24 months after acquisition). Claiming a SUE ITC reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the relevant CCA class in the following taxation year.
4.5 Proposed Budget 2026 Expansion: Regulatory Certification and IP Protection

Tabled on November 5, 2026, Federal Budget 2026 (Masters of our Destiny, print pp. 117, 402–403; PDF pp. 127, 420–421) proposes expanding eligible SR&ED expenditures—projected to deliver $930,000,000 over five years and $235,000,000 per year ongoing—for expenditures incurred in taxation years that begin on or after Budget Day (November 5, 2026) (meaning a December 31 year-end corporation would first claim these costs for its taxation year starting January 1, 2027, subject to legislative enactment). Operating within existing SR&ED credit rates (35% enhanced / 15% basic), the proposal introduces two downstream commercialization categories directly tied to an eligible SR&ED project:

First, initial regulatory approval and certification testing covers "tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements" carried out for "obtaining the initial approval or certification necessary to commercialize a product or process" (benefiting medical devices, health/food products, aerospace/automotive components, cleantech, and safety-certified electrical equipment). Claimable costs follow standard SR&ED categories (wages, materials, contracts, overhead, and machinery/equipment), while routine quality control, post-approval market testing, and recertifications do not qualify.

Second, intellectual property registration and maintenance covers costs reasonably incurred to obtain and maintain IP protection—including preparing and filing applications and paying periodic maintenance fees in Canada or abroad, provided the support activities occur in Canada—for IP developed in the course of an eligible SR&ED project across four IP types: patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and registered copyrights in software. Patent infringement litigation and enforcement costs are excluded, recapture rules will claw back related SR&ED deductions and ITCs if the IP is later disposed of, and the CRA will publish sector-specific commercialization guidance.

body.text: 5. Government Assistance Stacking and Provincial/Territorial R&D Regimes
5.1 Government Assistance Interactions (NRC IRAP and Provincial Credits)

Canadian R&D performers routinely stack federal SR&ED tax credits alongside direct federal grants (such as NRC IRAP non-repayable R&D labour contributions) and provincial or territorial R&D tax credits. Under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy and section 127, both government assistance (including NRC IRAP grants and provincial R&D tax credits) and non-government assistance or contract payments reduce the taxpayer's federal qualified SR&ED expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar before the federal 15% or 35% ITC is computed (with capital assistance/contract payments reported on Form T661 Line 518 and non-arm's-length allocated assistance reported on Line 540 via Form T1145). Despite this dollar-for-dollar expenditure pool grind, stacking NRC IRAP, provincial R&D credits, and the 35% federal SR&ED credit (amplified by the 55% PPA on eligible wages) substantially lowers net after-tax R&D cash outlay.
5.2 Québec's 2025–2026 Consolidation: The CRIC, CDAEIA, and C3i Regimes

Administered independently by Revenu Québec, Québec's innovation tax landscape underwent a sweeping structural overhaul in the March 25, 2025 Québec Budget (2025–2026). Effective for taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec introduced the Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation (CRIC), replacing eight legacy fiscal measures. Specifically, Québec abolished six corporate R&D and design tax credits—(1) the R&D salaries and wages credit (14% base / 30% enhanced on Form RD-1029.7-V, which continues to apply only to taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025); (2) the university, public research centre, or research consortium contract credit (Form RD-1029.8.6-V); (3) the research consortium fees and dues credit; (4) the private partnership pre-competitive research credit; (5) the technological adaptation services credit; and (6) the industrial design component of the in-house design credit (preserving fashion design)—while also abolishing the personal income tax holidays for foreign researchers and foreign experts. To support CRIC subcontracting claims, Québec amended the Act respecting the sectoral parameters of certain fiscal measures so the Minister of the Economy, Innovation and Energy continues certifying eligible public research centres and research consortia, and the Minister of Finance continues recognizing eligible university entities.

Claimed via Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (RD-1029.8.CR, alongside Form RD-222-V for Québec R&D deductions), the CRIC is 100% refundable in cash for all eligible corporations operating a business with an establishment in Québec—regardless of asset size, revenue, public listing, or foreign ownership. The CRIC pays 30% on the first $1,000,000 of net qualified expenditures exceeding an annual exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 tier, with no upper expenditure ceiling. The annual exclusion threshold equals the greater of $50,000 or the sum across eligible employees of the Québec personal income tax basic personal amount (for example, $18,571 per employee in 2025 as noted in practitioner guidance), adjusted for the proportion of time each employee spends on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization work.

Crucially, the CRIC covers not only basic research, applied research, and experimental development in Québec, but also pre-commercialization activities carried out in conjunction with Québec R&D: (a) regulatory tests, technological validations, and studies aimed at obtaining initial commercialization approval or certification, and (b) product design (form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials). Qualified CRIC expenditures (reduced by any government or non-government grants) include 100% of Québec employee wages, 100% of depreciable property/equipment acquisition costs (excluding buildings, land, rights to use buildings/land, and Large Investment Project tax-holiday assets), 50% of Québec subcontractor contracts, and 50% of payments to recognized Québec public research centres, consortia, or university entities. CRIC equipment claims cannot be stacked on the same asset with Québec's refundable C3i (Crédit d'impôt pour investissement et innovation—paying 15%, 20%, or 25% by region on manufacturing equipment, computer hardware, and management software above $5,000 or $12,500 per property up to a $100,000,000 four-year cap). As of November 2026, CRA policy listing four former Québec R&D credits as federal government assistance had not yet been updated to explicitly address the CRIC.

In parallel, Québec overhauled its IT salary credit: the CDAE (30% total: 23% refundable + 7% non-refundable for fiscal years starting in 2025) was replaced for fiscal years starting after December 31, 2025 by the CDAEIA, requiring an annual Investissement Québec certificate confirming significant artificial intelligence (AI) integration (adding AI data processing/hosting while removing routine maintenance/evolution). Above an exclusion threshold, the CDAEIA provides a 30% credit split 22% refundable + 8% non-refundable in 2026, 21% + 9% in 2027, and 20% + 10% from 2028 onward (halved in certain ≥50% non-arm's-length scenarios).
5.3 Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Yukon, and Other Jurisdictions

Across Canada's 13 provinces and territories, nine provinces plus Yukon offer R&D tax credits that stack with federal SR&ED, whereas three jurisdictions (Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut) offer no provincial or territorial R&D tax credit.

Ontario administers three stackable corporate credits through the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario): (1) the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — section 96, subsections 96(3.1), 96(8), and 96(12)), an 8% fully refundable credit on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit that remained at $3,000,000 in 2026 (maximum $240,000 refundable credit, phased out on prior-year taxable income and taxable capital, with an elective waiver available under subsection 96(14)); (2) the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), a 3.5% non-refundable credit with no expenditure cap; and (3) the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), a 20% fully refundable credit on qualified contracts with eligible Ontario research institutes.

British Columbia provides a 10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit. In its 2026 provincial budget, British Columbia removed the credit's statutory sunset date and fully harmonized with federal Bill C-15 effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024: raising the BC refundable expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, expanding the taxable capital phase-out band from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, reinstating capital expenditure eligibility, extending refundable BC SR&ED eligibility to ECPCs, and announcing 2026 consultations with stakeholders and Ottawa on introducing a BC patent box regime for the life sciences sector.

Alberta administers the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) directly on the Alberta corporate tax return (occasionally mislabelled as "AITC" in non-primary vendor summaries). Open to corporations regardless of foreign control, the IEG provides an 8% fully refundable base credit on eligible Alberta R&D spending and up to 20% refundable on incremental spending exceeding the corporation's prior two-year Alberta R&D average, capped at $4,000,000 of annual spending and phased out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of taxable capital.
Saskatchewan provides a 10% R&D tax credit, and Yukon provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit plus an additional 5% (20% total) on eligible payments to Yukon University.

body.text: 6. Filing Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, Penalties, and Audit Defence
6.1 Statutory Deadlines, Prescribed Tax Forms, and Processing Standards

Under subsection 37(11) of the ITA, taxpayers face a rigid 18-month reporting deadline after the end of the fiscal year in which SR&ED expenditures were incurred to file prescribed technical and financial forms. For a corporation with a December 31, 2025 fiscal year-end, its T2 corporate income tax return is due June 30, 2026, and its absolute SR&ED filing deadline is June 30, 2027. Beyond 18 months, the SR&ED claim is permanently statute-barred with no statutory extensions. Filing the SR&ED package concurrently with the original corporate tax return accelerates cash recovery: the CRA maintains a 60-day service standard for processing refundable claims accepted as filed, achieving 95.0% compliance in fiscal year 2025/26.

Claimants must file the updated federal forms issued by the CRA on May 15, 2026 (incorporating Bill C-15's post-December 15, 2024 rules): Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, read alongside Guide T4088); Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)) or, for corporations, Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations); Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance, excluding Line 390 ASA property and adjusting UCC for Line 504 SUE ITCs); and, where applicable within non-arm's-length groups, Form T1145 (assistance allocation) and Form T1146 (qualified contract expenditure transfer). Québec claimants additionally attach Form RD-1029.8.CR-T and Form RD-222-V (or legacy Forms RD-1029.7-V / RD-1029.8.6-V for taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025).
6.2 CRA Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

Following the October 2024 rollout of the My Business Account SR&ED client portal and pre-claim workbook, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026. This mechanism enables eligible businesses—specifically CCPCs, other Canadian corporations, or partnerships that have gross business income under $25,000,000 and are in good tax-compliance standing with the CRA—to determine whether planned projects qualify technically for SR&ED before starting work or incurring costs. Submitted through My Business Account, applications receive a formal CRA eligibility determination within eight weeks, supported by one-on-one CRA outreach sessions (OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca), Microsoft Teams webinars, and updated review procedures in The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants.
6.3 Claim Preparer Penalties and Seven-Step Audit Defence Protocol

Under Part 9 of Form T661 and subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3) of the ITA, complete and accurate claim preparer information must be disclosed on every SR&ED filing. Subsection 162(5.1) imposes a $1,000 penalty whenever a false statement or omission occurs in Part 9 claim preparer disclosures, and the external claim preparer and the claimant are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable for that penalty (subject to the preparer due-diligence relief rule in subsection 162(5.2)). Furthermore, aggressive or unsupported filings risk triggering CRA gross negligence penalties. To safeguard claims under appellate standards and the 2025–2026 statutory rules, claimants should implement the following seven-step audit protocol:

items: Use Pre-Claim Approval Strategically: Eligible Canadian corporations and partnerships with gross business income under $25,000,000 should apply via My Business Account eight weeks ahead of launching novel or high-budget R&D initiatives.

Maintain Contemporaneous Evidence (Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 5): Never rely on a posteriori narratives reconstructed after year-end. Capture dated hypotheses, experimental test logs, failure analyses, and logical conclusions generated contemporaneously as work progresses.

Segregate Project Time Contemporaneously: Track regular and specified-employee SR&ED hours by discrete project, isolating qualifying experimental development from routine engineering, commercial production, or quality control.

Audit Post-December 15, 2024 Equipment Acquisitions and Machine Logs: Verify acquisition/available-for-use dates after December 15, 2024, back out used equipment on Form T661 Line 532, omit Line 390 ASA assets from Schedule T2SCH8, and keep 12- and 24-month operating-time logs proving >50% SR&ED usage for Line 504 SUE claims.

Evaluate the CCPC Gross Revenue Phase-Out Election: Whenever associated prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 while three-year average gross revenue is lower, elect the ECPC revenue-based phase-out method under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) to protect the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit.

Tag Regulatory Certification and IP Protection Costs by Project: Beginning now for taxation years starting on or after November 5, 2026, isolate initial regulatory validation studies and patent/software-copyright filing and maintenance invoices in project-level sub-ledgers ahead of Budget 2026 enactment.
Verify Form T661 Part 9 Disclosures: Audit all third-party preparer details in Part 9 prior to filing to eliminate $1,000 penalty exposure under subsection 162(5.1).

body.text: 7. International Tax Interaction: Pillar Two and Canada's Global Minimum Tax Act
7.1 Scope, Charging Rules, and Safe Harbours Under the GMTA

Multinational Enterprise (MNE) groups performing R&D in Canada must account for Canada's Global Minimum Tax Act (GMTA, S.C. 2024, c. 17, s. 81, enacted via Bill C-69), which received Royal Assent on June 20, 2024 and incorporates the OECD/G20 Pillar Two Global Anti-Base Erosion (GloBE) Model Rules and Commentary. The GMTA applies to MNE groups operating in Canada and at least one foreign jurisdiction with consolidated annual revenues of €750,000,000 or more in at least two of the four preceding fiscal years.

In-scope MNEs must compute their jurisdictional Effective Tax Rate (Effective Tax Rate = Adjusted Covered Taxes ÷ Net GloBE Income) on a country-by-country basis against a 15% minimum ETR. Where the Canadian jurisdictional ETR falls below 15%, top-up tax applies (after deducting a substance-based income exclusion based on Canadian tangible assets and payroll costs) through three charging mechanisms: a Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-Up Tax (QDMTT) giving Canada primary domestic taxing rights and an Income Inclusion Rule (IIR) for Canadian parent entities, both effective for fiscal years beginning on or after December 31, 2023; and a backstop Undertaxed Profits Rule (UTPR) introduced in Bill C-31, effective for fiscal years beginning on or after December 31, 2025.

Initial GMTA returns, GloBE Information Returns (GIR), GIR Notifications, and top-up tax payments became due starting June 30, 2026 (standard deadline of 15 months post-fiscal year-end, with an 18-month transitional window for the initial reporting year). Entities must keep GMTA records for eight years, facing late-filing penalties of $25,000 per complete month up to 40 months ($1,000,000 maximum) for unfiled GIRs/notifications plus 5% on unpaid IIR/DMTT tax. Temporary and permanent safe harbours replicated in the GMTA include the Transitional CbCR Safe Harbour (requiring either <€10,000,000 revenue and <€1,000,000 pre-tax profit under the de minimis test, or a simplified ETR of ≥15% pre-2025, ≥16% in 2025, and ≥17% for fiscal years beginning after December 31, 2025), the Permanent QDMTT Safe Harbour, and a five-year initial international activity exemption (≤6 jurisdictions and ≤€50,000,000 net book value of foreign tangible assets outside the largest jurisdiction).
7.2 Impact of Non-Refundable vs. Refundable Canadian R&D Credits on GloBE ETR

Under the GMTA and OECD Pillar Two rules, non-refundable tax credits (which are neither cash-refundable Qualified Refundable Tax Credits [QRTCs] nor Marketable Transferable Tax Credits transferable to an unrelated purchaser within 15 months of the origination year under section 2 of the GMTA) directly reduce Adjusted Covered Taxes in the numerator of the GloBE ETR fraction—meaning generous non-refundable R&D credits or accelerated write-offs can push an MNE's Canadian jurisdictional ETR below 15% and trigger Canadian QDMTT top-up tax that claws back part of the tax incentive.

Because any MNE group exceeding €750,000,000 in consolidated revenue (or any foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiary) sits above the $75,000,000 phase-out ceiling or outside Canadian-control rules, its 15% federal SR&ED ITC and 3.5% Ontario ORDTC are 100% non-refundable and non-transferable. Consequently, large MNEs claiming substantial non-refundable 15% federal SR&ED ITCs must model whether their Canadian Adjusted Covered Taxes remain above the 15% GloBE floor (or 17% 2026 Transitional CbCR Safe Harbour threshold), relying on their Canadian R&D payroll and lab equipment substance-based income exclusion to shelter excess profits from QDMTT clawback. Conversely, 100% cash-refundable provincial R&D credits open to large and foreign-owned MNEs—led by Québec's CRIC (30% / 20%) alongside Ontario's 20% OBRITC and Yukon's 15% credit—deliver cash support without requiring tax liability, positioning them far more favourably under Pillar Two QRTC principles. Finally, as 2026 Canadian economic policy research highlights, because the international Pillar Two Side-by-Side (SbS) compromise shields US-headquartered MNEs from key Pillar Two burdens while leaving Canadian-headquartered MNEs subject to the full compliance and ETR mechanics of the GMTA, in-scope Canadian multinationals face heightened urgency in coordinating SR&ED claims with annual Pillar Two ETR modelling.
